CommentText: I'd like to know the rationale behind using these specific patterns. It heavily relies on the software's nature in determining the appropriate patterns. Moreover, a significant caveat is that improperly applied abstractions, such as design patterns, irritate people and make the software more rigid. Consequently, developers tend to circumvent them, worsening the situation. Also, the vague explanation of 'leaky abstraction' leaves much to be desired, and I believe it's confusing to many. It essentially means implementation details are showing up at a higher level of abstraction. If you use an ORM to perform database CRUD operations, the underlying driver for MySQL, Postgres, or others shouldn't appear in either your code or the ORM. A leak can also occur if lower-level implementation details are accessible by something that should not have access. I think people should understand SOLID and the principles it represents before applying GoF design patterns.

First of all I will separate the nine balls into 2 group ,one containing 5 ball and the other containing 4 balls .Then, I will put them on the balance on the either side .
Now,there can be two cases which could occur here
1)THE LIGHTER BALL IS IN GROUP OF 5 BALLS
If this happens then the balance will weigh approximately equal on both side . After that I will transfer one ball from group 5 to group 4 and if the balance disturbs then that ball is heavier one and if the balance remain as it is then that ball is a lighter one.If the ball is found to be a heavier one then I will put it back to group of 5 balls and will try for another one till the balance does not disturb while transferring the ball
2)THE LIGHTER BALL IS IN THE GROUP OF 4 BALLS
Since, the group of 4 balls contain the lighter ball the balance will weigh more on the side where 5 balls are placed i.e unequal. Now the thing we gonna do this is to exchange the ball  of group 4 with group 5 and if the balance still remains unequal then both the balls exchanged were heavier hence no change in reading and then we will put the balls back to their places  . If the balance becomes approximately equal then then we can say that the ball which was transferred from group of 4 is the lighter one .

CommentText: I believe this is more beneficial for generating programming ideas than programming for you. For instance, suppose you want to create an application or game that can detect if the user entered an offensive word or phrase as their name. It seems simple on the surface, but if you create a program that tries to check every possible combination (within a specified character limit), it will have unnecessary checks and be unoptimized. It may not consider checking only combinations that match the length of the user's input. Users might attempt to bypass the program by substituting letters with numbers, such as replacing a lowercase "L" with "1". Additionally, it may not know whether you want to support all languages, multiple languages, or just one language, as some offensive words are not universal or can be unique to one language but foreign to another. Furthermore, some real names "technically" contain curse words. Also, if someone named Richard enters his name as "Dick," the program may not assume or consider that it is a nickname. You can't anticipate every logical scenario or assume what is ideal to meet a user's needs, especially those with complex layers and specific/unique situations.

CommentText:
I'm thinking you can just invert the frequencyMap to {frequency: list of values with that frequency} and then sort the keys in that inverted map. This sorting would be O(sqrt(n) log(sqrt(n))) (which is < O(n)) because there cannot be more than O(sqrt(n)) different frequencies (if each value has a different frequency, then n = O(c * (c+1) /2), with c being the number of distinct frequencies). 
Then it's just a matter of iterating over the reverse sorted keys and adding values to a resultArray until that array reaches length k


        lookupDict = defaultdict(int)
        for n in nums:
            lookupDict[n] += 1
            
        inverseDict = defaultdict(list)
        for key, v in lookupDict.items():
            inverseDict[v].append(key)        
        sortedKeys = sorted(inverseDict.keys(), reverse = True)
        sortedKeysIndex = 0 
        
        res = []
        while k > 0:
            values = inverseDict[sortedKeys[sortedKeysIndex]]
            if len(values) > k:
                res.extend(values[:k])
            else:
                res.extend(values)
            k -= len(values)
            sortedKeysIndex += 1
       return res

CommentText:
After reading and watching the interviews with Tony last week speaking about his last shoot--the Hong Kong episode, things seem clearer to me. He had tried for years to get his idol, the legendary cinematographer Christopher Doyle, to appear in an episode. Not only did he appear, but he got behind the camera and actually photographed the entire episode. To add to the serendipity, his director had an emergency illness 2 days before the shoot. He asked his girlfriend Asia Argento to step in and direct it. She did. And all this happened in Hong Kong--Tony's favorite location. It was truly the pinnacle of his career. Could it EVER get any better...

I know Tony loved his friends and his family, but I think his career (Not the money nor the fame, but the PASSION for what he did) was his life. He lived life hard and passionatly, yet with great sensitivity, and sometimes that passion can drain you over time--especially when you reach a perceived pinnacle that you fear you may never reach again. I think Hong Kong was, in his mind, as good as it could get, and as good as it was ever going to be.

CommentText:
Claiming that the 5070 is equal to or better than the 4090 is misleading for several reasons. 

First, looking at the specs, the 4090 outperforms the 5070 in nearly every area except memory speed. For me, the extra memory on the 4090 is crucial because I play at high resolutions with max settings, and the types of games I enjoy require more than 12GB of VRAM. While 12GB might be sufficient for lower resolutions or settings, it’s just one example of where the 5070 falls short.

Second, not all games support DLSS frame generation. For instance, I play *Star Citizen*, which doesn’t offer it, and *Ark: Ascended*, where it was previously available but has been removed (likely due to latency issues). Frame generation isn’t supported in most of the games I play, so for me, the 5070 would be a noticeable downgrade. And even when frame generation is available, it introduces artifacting and added latency, which I personally find distracting. For example, in *Ark: Ascended*, I preferred lowering settings and playing at a lower FPS rather than dealing with the latency from frame generation.

Lastly, I think we can all agree that there’s no good reason why higher-tier 40-series cards like the 4090 don’t support DLSS 4. The 4090 has more AI cores than the 5070, so it should theoretically benefit even more from DLSS 4 if it were enabled.

That said, for more casual gamers playing DLSS 4-supported titles, the 5070 might be a great option. But it’s dishonest to suggest it’s better than the 4090, especially for someone like me who relies on the performance and features the 4090 delivers. The 5070 simply doesn’t come close to matching what I get from my 4090 in the games I play.

You can skip the first if condition by doing this:
Instead of comparing mid pointer with left, compare it with right (all other factors remain same).

For example: [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]
Iteration 1:
start pointer (s) = 0
end pointer (e) = 6
mid pointer (m) = (s+e)//2 =3 
here, nums[m] >= nums[e]:
therefore,    s=m+1

Iteration 2
s=4
e=9
m = 5
here, nums[m]<nums[e]
therefore, e=mid-1

Iteration 3:
s=4
e=4
mid=4
Here, we are at the minimum element so return it

This change is used to tackle an edge case where we are already in a sorted array. (hence removing the if condition)
In this example, at iteration 2, subarray [0,1,2] is sorted. If we checked mid pointer with left we would get subarray [2] but we checked mid pointer with right so we got sub array [0]

Fascist regimes tend to make constant use of patriotic mottos, slogans, symbols, songs, and other paraphernalia. Flags are seen everywhere, as are flag symbols on clothing and in public displays.

Disdain for the Recognition of Human Rights

Because of fear of enemies and the need for security, the people in fascist regimes are persuaded that human rights can be ignored in certain cases because of "need." The people tend to look the other way or even approve of torture, summary executions, assassinations, long incarcerations of prisoners, etc.

Identification of Enemies/Scapegoats as a Unifying Cause

The people are rallied into a unifying patriotic frenzy over the need to eliminate a perceived common threat or foe: racial, ethnic or religious minorities; liberals; communists; socialists, terrorists, etc.

Supremacy of the Military

Even when there are widespread domestic problems, the military is given a disproportionate amount of government funding, and the domestic agenda is neglected. Soldiers and military service are glamorized.

Rampant Sexism

The governments of fascist nations tend to be almost exclusively male-dominated. Under fascist regimes, traditional gender roles are made more rigid. Opposition to abortion is high, as is homophobia and anti-gay legislation and national policy.

Controlled Mass Media

Sometimes the media is directly controlled by the government, but in other cases, the media is indirectly controlled by government regulation, or sympathetic media spokespeople and executives. Censorship, especially in war time, is very common.

Obsession with National Security

Fear is used as a motivational tool by the government over the masses.

Religion and Government are Intertwined

Governments in fascist nations tend to use the most common religion in the nation as a tool to manipulate public opinion. Religious rhetoric and terminology is common from government leaders, even when the major tenets of the religion are diametrically opposed to the government's policies or actions.

Corporate Power is Protected

The industrial and business aristocracy of a fascist nation often are the ones who put the government leaders into power, creating a mutually beneficial business/government relationship and power elite.

Labor Power is Suppressed

Because the organizing power of labor is the only real threat to a fascist government, labor unions are either eliminated entirely, or are severely suppressed.

Disdain for Intellectuals and the Arts

Fascist nations tend to promote and tolerate open hostility to higher education, and academia. It is not uncommon for professors and other academics to be censored or even arrested. Free expression in the arts is openly attacked, and governments often refuse to fund the arts.

Obsession with Crime and Punishment

Under fascist regimes, the police are given almost limitless power to enforce laws. The people are often willing to overlook police abuses and even forego civil liberties in the name of patriotism. There is often a national police force with virtually unlimited power in fascist nations.

Rampant Cronyism and Corruption

Fascist regimes almost always are governed by groups of friends and associates who appoint each other to government positions and use governmental power and authority to protect their friends from accountability. It is not uncommon in fascist regimes for national resources and even treasures to be appropriated or even outright stolen by government leaders.

Fraudulent Elections

Sometimes elections in fascist nations are a complete sham. Other times elections are manipulated by smear campaigns against or even assassination of opposition candidates, use of legislation to control voting numbers or political district boundaries, and manipulation of the media. 11:20 This is a tiny computer science detail and probably not relevant for coding interviews, but just changing the data structure from a deque to a stack does not make BFS an iterative DFS as far as I know. If you do that, the algorithm is still correct but the order in which the nodes are visited is not the same as true DFS. What you also need to make it a true DFS (in terms of visit order) is, delay checking whether a node is visited until you actually pop the node. This way, some nodes are added to the stack twice, but they're checked when they are popped so the algorithm is correct + the order is truly DFS.

From wiki: "The non-recursive implementation is similar to breadth-first search but differs from it in two ways: it uses a stack instead of a queue, and it delays checking whether a vertex has been discovered until the vertex is popped from the stack rather than making this check before adding the vertex."


Some relevant reading material: "BFS vs DFS, and Timing of Marking Vertex as Visited" from cs stackexchange.

CommentText:
This video is very well done. Well-scripted. Well-presented. Factually accurate. Kudos.

Of this list, my favourite is Go. I've used JavaScript, Python, Java, and C++, and I don't like any of them. I understand *why* they are popular (strong libraries, plentiful job opportunities), but none of them are pleasant to use.

JavaScript is a very sloppy and undisciplined language full of potholes and dark corners. Python, while easy to learn, is not much better.

Java feels like a straightjacket and C++ is mind-numbingly complicated.

That said, my favourite programming language, bar none, is Smalltalk. While it's not very popular, it has enormous advantages:

- Smalltalk is very, very simple and easy to learn (much more so than Python) — the complete syntax fits on a post card!
- Thus, Smalltalk imposes a virtually nonexistent cognitive load on the programmer.
- Smalltalk is the purest and most elegant of OOP languages. This makes writing large, scalable systems relatively painless.
- By using TDD, Smalltalk is safe, reliable, and maintainable.
- Smalltalk's image-based development system offers many benefits — it's comparable to containerized software like Docker.
- Smalltalk is the most productive programming language — you can typically write a Smalltalk application in a fraction of the time it would take in Python, JavaScript, and Java.
- Smalltalk is extremely flexible and versatile — it can be used for web, AI, data science, IoT, VR/AR, enterprise, etc.

I love this language to pieces. For more information, visit smalltalk.tech.blog.

CommentText: As is typical with hyped technologies, it's crucial to acknowledge their limitations. Microservices, for instance, present significant orchestration challenges. When deploying A, does B also need deployment? Is API versioning necessary? Such considerations introduce complexity absent in monolithic systems. Specifically, the use of separate databases incurs a substantial overhead. SQL's querying power and features like cascade delete are lost, and cross-database communication is slower due to network overhead. Serverless architectures, with their on-demand nature, suffer from 'cold start' issues. If a function initializes with every infrequent event, like hourly newsletter signups, users experience delays. These problems have solutions, but avoid blindly applying new technologies to every project simply because it's trending.

CommentText: This is why reading up on the engine your rebuilding is important, split crankcase type blocks can be tricky and the days of a simple main cap is going away. Tolerances are so much tighter on modern engines and especially something like a GT3RS, I am sure u have made a couple engine builder friends in the car world by now after doing this so long. Looking at the factory Porsche manual it outlines everything u had to learn the hard way :), being from the old school of mechanics we actually read paper manuals but today its all PDF unless u wanna pay a arm and a leg for it. You got really lucky that nothing worse happened and damage was minimal,  learned a valuable lesson that will never be forgotten and gained more experience with your engine. Knowing your car inside and out is super important and gets even crazier the higher end the car is, Many of the top engines for high end cars are hand built like AMG, GTR, ect. They may be hand built but the torquing of bolts along with RTV gasket sealer application is done by robot, its so cool to watch and built many higher end motors myself over the years but i have a excellent engine builder/machine shop owner as a close friend. Learned so much from him and so many late nights at the shop helping him just listening to the knowledge, whenever i am stumped on a motor issue i can give him a ring for a little guidance. Sucks u had to do the job twice Matt but these things happen and your just gaining more experience, you should be super proud of what u have done with this car and the engine alone was a huge accomplishment. Cant wait for the next crazy build after this bro, you have worked hard to get to this point and deserve it all. Just nice to see a good dude and his dad plus friends helping him build these cars, Matts dad is awesome and reminds me a lot of my dad with his humor and skill. There are many that do rebuilds on youtube but a reason we watch u bud, Its getting there and will be done soon enough. Oh and that dual mass flywheel was trash, many times we swap dual mass back to single with a kit but just depends on your needs and power level. Good thing u got a new one though, that old one would have made noise for sure.

CommentText: If anyone's finding the Maths Generator confusing around Line 19: the terms 'expr' and 'answer' are NOT related to those terms inside the function (on line 15). They're completely new variables, defined externally to the function, that simply share the same names as those within the function. To see this, try misspelling the words (from line 19 onwards, consistently), and you'll notice they aren't connected to 'expr' and 'answer' on line 15. In that context on L15, they only serve as placeholders for the function's two return values. You can initialize them with totally different names... this probably makes it even more confusing! :-o

CommentText: Above 4G decoding is fine because it just allows 64 bit OSes to access more than 4GBs of system memory on 64 bit systems, but SAM can actually cause system instability and display crashing. I’ve had nothing but driver timeouts when SAM is enabled on a driver level. What SAM does is that it enables the CPU to process more than 256MBs of GPU memory per window. Usually, your GPU’s memory allocation is split into multiple windows of memory. SAM just allows for all the memory to be allocated into one single window. This is bad, not good. It means that if you play memory intensive games, your GPU will crash when it runs out of memory. Regardless if you have enough system memory or a page file set up. SAM should be enabled on a case by case scenario.

CommentText: I doubt I could have devised the NC solution in an interview setting. The best I could manage was employing a hash function: def groupAnagrams(strs: List[str]) -> List[List[str]]: hash_index_map = collections.defaultdict(list) for i, word in enumerate(strs): hash_value = 0 for char in word: hash_value += hash(str(ord(char))) hash_index_map[hash_value].append(strs[i]) return hash_index_map.values() This code gets through all LC checks, although it's not completely reliable due to the possibility of different words having the same hash value. This probably wouldn't pass in an interview. In a real-world scenario, I'd likely use: def group_anagrams(strings): res = defaultdict(list) for s in strings: res[tuple(sorted(s))].append(s) return res.values() and be done with it.

CommentText:
Trump has a PhD in unbridled buffoonery.

In 2005, Timothy O’Brien, then a reporter for the New York Times, had published a book called “Trump Nation: The Art of Being the Donald.” In the book, O’Brien cited people who questioned a claim at the bedrock of Trump’s identity — that his net worth was more than $5 billion. O’Brien said he had spoken to three people who estimated that the figure was between $150 million and $250 million. 

Trump sued. He later told The Post that he intended to hurt O’Brien, whom he called a “lowlifeSleazebag.” 

By filing suit, Trump hadn’t just opened himself up to questioning — he had opened a door into the opaque and secretive company he ran. 

The lawsuit had given O’Brien's attorneys the power to request that Trump turn over internal company documents, and they used it. They arrived at the deposition having already identified where Trump’s public statements hadn’t matched the private truth. 

Trump may not have realized it yet, but he had walked into a trap. 

Trump had brought it on himself. He had sued a reporter, accusing him of being reckless and dishonest in a book that raised questions about Trump’s net worth. The reporter’s attorneys turned the tables and brought Trump in for a deposition. 

For two straight days, they asked Trump question after question that touched on the same theme: Trump’s honesty. 

The lawyers confronted Trump with his own past statements — and with his company’s internal documents, which often showed those statements had been patently false or invented. The lawyers were relentless. Trump was vulnerable — cornered, sweating, unprepared, and under oath. 

Thirty times, they caught him.
Trump had lied about sales at his condo buildings. Inflated the price of membership at one of his golf clubs. Overstated the depth of his past debts and the number of his employees. 

That deposition — 170 transcribed pages — offers extraordinary insights into Trump’s relationship with the truth. Trump’s lies were unstrategic — needless, highly specific, easy to disprove. When caught, Trump sometimes blamed others for the error or explained that the untrue thing really was true, at least in his mind. 

“A very clear and visible side effect of my lawyers’ questioning of Trump is that he was revealed as a routine and habitual fabulist,” said Timothy O’Brien.

CommentText:
So I'm pretty against design patterns in the way they are taught, because most if not all of that stuff is either common sense when you encounter a specific problem or unnecessary boilerplate for a simple problem which doesn't need added complexity to be solved. I'm trying to give them a chance, but already at the Memento pattern I have a big issue with it. To use the EditorState and History classes you still have to store their instances inside Editor if you want them to be used by Editor methods, so you're basically doing the same thing as just storing a list of states inside Editor, but you've added some unnecessary boilerplate. You could also pass History to the Editor, but them you have some very unnecessary coupling with the caller of Editor.createState having to know about the History.

In the language of design patterns, I would've created a 'facade' to hide the History interaction behind a 'EditorWithHistory', but in reality that would land me at step 1 after adding two unnecessary layers of abstraction. You see what I mean?

If a system is too complex, we add abstraction which simplifies the understanding of the system with respect to some specific target (team members working on the code, integration with some other system, fitting with a specific framework, making the code easy to verify with regard to fulfilling given requirements, being easy to understand or to use by the end user, etc.) and the kind of abstraction we use will depend on that specific target we have independently of any arbitrary set of solutions chosen from the design patterns. And if abstraction isn't necessary, then we don't mention it, we don't think about it - it doesn't exist as applied to the specific problem we're working on. So just teaching this stuff in the way where developers are supposed to know the names, types, examples etc. seems backwards to me. If someone likes to work with solutions in this framework - that's fine, but I don't see why it's forced upon developers if they don't need to store a problem-solution manual in their head to solve the actual problems they encounter. That's obviously not a critique of the learning resources, but the expectation that a developer should learn this to somehow be a 'complete' developer.

Your x-coordinate calculations don't verify collisions after the velocity update. As a result, the program fails when the large block moves far enough, entering the wall.  The glitches are being hidden by limiting the drawing position and using manual increments of the time steps to prevent it from occurring. The issue won't go away by these methods. The x-coordinate should not be updated until all of the large block's momentum has transferred through the small block to the wall. A while loop should be used instead of a for loop, with calculations repeating until the large block's velocity becomes positive. The timing of the animation is not relevant; by using set amounts of for loop repetitions, it's hoped that the large block doesn't pass through the smaller block. It should instead be calculated as often as needed using a while loop. Using a while loop will cause the program to freeze until the large block's momentum is transferred. CommentText:
The dynamic programming solution to me is more intuitive. Neetcode explains in the drawing but the names chosen for variables are lacking in meaning which impacts the clarity of the solution in code (e.g. "dp" stands for dynamic programming I suppose which isn't very helpful IMO). What is actually being stored in "dp" is the number of ways we can decode an input that starts with dp[i]. So a better name for dp might be "decodeCount". 

And then we have 3 cases:

s[i] is "0" in which case there are 0 ways to decode an input that starts with "0"
Here decodeCount[i] = 0
* For instance, if we look at the substring "0123" from "10123", from i=1 there are 0 ways to decode "0123" because we can't have a leading zero at the beginning of our input

s[i] is non-zero and cannot be used to form a valid 2 digit number. That is, our prior decodeCount simply carries over
Here decodeCount[i] = decodeCount[i + 1]
*If this doesn't make sense consider an input like "999", there is exactly 1 way to decode this input and because we never discover a valid 2 digit number, this never changes

s[i] is non-zero, and forms a valid 2 digit number starting with "1" or "2"
Here decodeCount[i] = decodeCount[i + 1] + decodeCount[i + 2]

*All the ways we can decode starting at s[i +1] are still valid if we treat s[i] as a single digit, but we need to also count an additional decodeCount[i + 2] ways because we can also use 2 digits starting at s[i]

* Example: "129" gives us (1, 2, 9), (12, 9) as valid decodings (2 total). At s[0] we need to count decodeCount[1] which is 1, and decodeCount[2] which is 1, which accounts for the case of starting with "1" and starting with "12".

I know I can get a decent support role job but no coz I know I will slack during job which I don't want now. No more slacking now. Now is the time to build solid foundations. If you are starting out, below points will help(also writing to remind myself from time to time):

1) Work really hard on building solid foundations especially about time complexity, searching, sorting, recursion and arrays. Don't move to other DS before doing this. You will be surprised and bit humbled about how less you know about these topics and how are they used to solve problems.

2) You are starting out so no problem is EASY - Just coz a problem is tagged under easy section doesn't mean its easy for you or its beneath you. Your mind will trick you into skipping it but don't give in. Code even if you know the solution and read about others soln and how you can optimize. Similarly, don't get disheartened if you are not able to solve even the easy problems. Its OK. Building intuition and problem solving skills takes time. So just keep going and take a break and come back again. 

I want to write more but I guess you get the point. Also if you are also out of job, I know times are tough and its really bad out there but I assure you the sun will shine on you. Just keep sharpening your sword. I know god has really great plans for you and he/she is testing you so that you can become a better version of yourself. A version who is consistent, disciplined, focused, and who really knows his/her shit. Work hard and hang in there. We'll rise again.

This seems to be a clustering problem, where clusters are defined as sets of adjacent 1s (horiz and vert).
Initialize an empty dictionary which will store the positions of the 1s, along with their corresponding "cluster_id". 
The first 1 gets a cluster_id of 1, then its position is stored in the dictionary. Next time a 1 is found check if it's adjacent to the first 1. 
If so, assign its cluster_id = 1 else assign its cluster_id = 2. Repeat this process, assigning cluster_id as appropriate until the matrix is processed.

The lengths are simply the counts of all the unique cluster ids!

Whenever you are talking to someone if the person walks away many people will take that personally and feel hurt. It hurts our ego. The speaker gives two strategies to not take things personally:
	1) It isn't about me: If a speaker is hurt by someone using a smartphone during the presentation, then it might not be about him- the topic might not interest the listener or he might have received an important text or he might be taking notes. When a child is denied something and wails and says 'I hate you', we don't take it personally because we know that it is the child's anger speaking. Look at the other person's intention. 	2) It is about me: It is about your insecurities. When you are being criticized and you are hurt chances are that it is rooted in your childhood. Give yourself empathy. Speak up for yourself. By opening up without blaming them will increase the chances of them accommodating your needs.
	
People may attack you but you must remember that you will always keep your value. Speaker also appeals to the audience to take thing personally for the next few days and then test out these strategies.

CommentText:
The problem I find with this is he is making conclusion about engineering as a non-engineer. There are plenty of ways you could make wind turbines less harmful to birds. There ways to deal with the variable amounts of energy produced. There are ways to cope with the amount of land needed for solar. There are ways to cope with potential waste. There are ways to source raw materials better. His talk is predicated on the idea that renewables will remain static in their form.  

I’m not entirely against nuclear, but there is one thing nuclear doesn’t let you do: change your philosophy on how we use energy. Nuclear energy is attractive, because rather than actually thinking about whether we want to solve problems through good design (energy efficiency, passive heating and cooling, better town planning, zero waste streams) we can just continue to throw energy at problems without actually dealing with things intelligently and in harmony with nature. 

With nuclear we can kick the can down the road until we get into wars over sourcing nuclear fuel because the population has exploded. 

We can still divide the world into haves and have nots depending on who has the necessary resources to produce that sort of power. And this is the true reason people want to distract us away from renewables with spurious superficial arguments as to why they can never be environmentally friendly. I don’t think this is his reasoning, but it something that has sucked several people in, because they only care about one side of the equation. They want an easy answer. “Let’s not try and make renewables better, letter just produce more energy with a non-renewable sources that allows us to ignore everything else that is wrong with our environmental philosophy!”  

It’s a dangerous philosophy because it sounds like he’s really thinking about both sides of the coin, but he’s created a false dichotomy of renewable versus nuclear and not included how we use energy, how we design renewables and how we change our whole philosophy of energy and resources use. Using nuclear energy doesn’t magically stop pollution, habitat destruction, resource wars, etc.

CommentText: Having completed the entire course, I want to share my feedback. First off, I took an exam today and passed, having utilized this course along with a few lessons from a Google course and 96 questions from ExamTopics (though only about 10% of the exam questions came from there). I'm really frustrated that nearly half the entire course focuses on networking. I understand that the instructor is experienced in networking, but the course should be balanced and accessible to everyone. While some details are useful, it would suffice to cover maybe 5 main characteristics for each topic. (e.g., Interconnect for private connections, VPCs with subnets, Shared VPCs for sharing multiple VPCs). There's no requirement for low-level information. Other points: I believed this course was recorded in 2022, based on the published date, but it was actually from 2020, three years ago. 2023 should be the last year to learn from this course in my opinion since resources and services are evolving. The outdated information and some services no longer exist. Because of this, this course is lacking services which I have seen in the exam and in the exam dumps.  The exam might have changed since 2020 because I haven't seen any ML questions in 96 questions neither on my exam, therefore you don't need to focus that much on it (but you still should). GKE and Compute Engines are major test topics, they need more focus. Also IAM, and billing. In general, I enjoyed the course and I'm thankful for it, however, without extensive networking info, this course could be 10 hours long and not 20 which is a substantial time investment (if you don't care much about networking like many software engineers).

25:40 so here's the explanation and my understanding of this particular example ---
The onclick here requires a reference of a function so that it can call it when the click event occurs on corresponding button, we always pass reference in this type of situation to prevent the function to get executed immediately. 
But the problem is we can't just pass the reference of the function because as we know it requires the color in the form of parameter and we are noy storing the reference in variable like structure such as let refHolder = clickHandler; so we can't call the refHolder later with the color parameter later in code such as refHolder('blue'). 
In reality, we are giving the reference to onclick which doesn't have an in built functionality or human intelligence to call this clickHandler with argument based on the button. 
So now we actually have a tiny war between onclick() demanding a reference and clickHandler(color) which demands to be called with a parameter only otherwise error. 

Now in order to fullfill the demand of bith entities, we can we will indeed call the clickHandler() with color parameter passed ( demand fulfilled ) but at the same time we will do something that a reference is given to onClick function ( which it strictly demands ), we will return reference of an inner function which does the main work or logic( demand fulfilled ) ( Very important thing to note here is this could not have been achieved without the feature of lexical scoping )

CommentText: This brings back old memories. Here are some thoughts on increasing performance (excluding reprogramming in assembly language): 1- Use pre-computed sin and cos values as you proposed yourself. 2- Deleting the entire HGR buffer on every frame takes a lot of time. This cannot be done during VSYNC as someone suggested, not even with cycle counting. The filling of the 4K bank with 0 takes almost one second and is probably the largest contributor to the lack of performance. You suggested the solution, which is to redraw the existing lines in black. Just keep 2 arrays and flip among them as you draw each page, so you always have access to the previous points, and alternate the rotate sub-routine to use either one or the other array as input according to the page you are in. 3- You might look at the shape table functionality of Applesoft. These are Applesoft driven but machine language managed drawing routines, including draw, xdraw and rot. 4- Remove those multiplications by zero from the code. 5- You might consider using integer variables for the positions on screen (by using a % on the arrays definition). Integer calculations are much faster than floating point. Or if you are up to a nice challenge, use integer basic instead. It is faster, but the challenge will be the sin/cos multiplication without FP. 6- This is more of a stretch, but if you can find a pair of sin/cos that are very close to multiples of 2, or at least very close to integer amounts, you can use shift operations for multiplication.

Linguist here. Native fluency and master level are different concepts. For European languages, there is a scale from A1 to A2, B1, B2, C1 and finally C2. They represent different levels of speaking areas and skills, being A1 the basic fluency and C2 the academic one. A native speaker tends to be around B2 or C1, whilst the educated person (who has a bachelor degree, for instance) will probably speak a more sophisticated level of that language, which would be C2. Pronunciation is also different from accent. They are both connected, but having an accent doesn't make you worse speaker than a native person, on the contrary, it just shows one speaks other languages. The main point is if having an accent makes the other person confused or lead to misunderstandings, then you must correct it.
I agree with the other points he said. Exposure to the language is very important: read, write, listen and speak as most as you can. That's the only way to be really fluent.

CommentText:
I feel so relived; I'm finally learning this darn thing! Thank you for the tutorial. Thank you for taking the time to do this Gwen!

Edit: Upon reviewing the tutorial again, I'd like to say:

1. When creating a tutorial, you guys should _truly_ understand the importance of slowing down to the pace of the learner. In the beginning you walk us through a nice set of key terms (which was exceptional), then start mixing lots of advanced and beginner-level concepts together in your explanations, confusing the person that's watching the video. Slow down, explain like we're 5, that's why we're here.

2. To expand upon the issue of mixing things up I mentioned above, it's okay to keep a tutorial short, and add footnotes later if you think that the advanced concepts you're touching on are still worth being aware of. That way, the beginner can truly focus their attention on the basics, and then access the footnote only when they feel comfortable with the knowledge they've acquired thus far, making the content of your footnotes even more effective. After all, isn't good programming about being efficient? 

I used to get annoyed at being expected to take additional English classes as a Computer Science student, but now I understand why. I spent 4 hours yesterday debugging a Terminal issue, only to later realize that there was an "issue" because the person who created the how-to GitHub document instructed the reader to paste this code into the Terminal command line: 

*eval "$(ssh-agent exec -s)"*

They said to *paste* this command in the terminal (meaning: include the quotation marks). After 4 hours of learning about chmod, File Links, Groups, root directory, Inodes—things I knew NOTHING about prior to this, I resolved my problem by simply removing the quotation marks. 

Now, the arrogant developer might say, "Well that's obvious". No it's not! The person said "paste", meaning I would: 

- Select the piece of code
- Apply ctrl+c to it, for Windows (cmd+c on Mac)
- Go to the Terminal and apply ctrl+v/cmd+v

Either the tutorial should have been made like this: 

*eval $(ssh-agent exec -s)* ,  

or the person writing the document should I mentioned that the quotation marks need to be removed. 

As Software Engineering becomes more collaborative, programmers can no longer get away with being asocial, and communication impaired, so this is an area a lot more engineers need to start being proficient in .

CommentText:
If there’s gonna be a snow storm tonight, you probably need to set your alarm for every couple of hours to make sure the entrance doesn’t fill with wind blown snow, thereby cutting off your fresh air, i.e. oxygen. Scary stuff. In a snow hole in the Cairngorms, Scottish Highlands (like the White Mountains, NH) we were forecast to have an overnight blizzard so I set my alarm for midnight to check the entrance. We went to sleep around 8 or 9 and it was still peaceful outside. When I woke up at 12 it was all quiet so I thought maybe the bad weather hadn’t arrived yet but I summoned the willpower to get out of my sleeping bag and bivi bag, put on my jacket and boots to go and check anyway. Lucky I did, rounding the corner (plenty corners, as highlighted in the video) I realised with horror the entrance was completely blocked with wind blown snow, hence the silence. It took me 10 min to shovel enough snow to make an air hole and the snow was filling in nearly as quick as I could shovel. At least with a hole I could now push the snow out rather than having to drag it in. It took around 45 min to clear the hole and fashion a kind of roof/lip so that more snow blew over the top and not into the entranceway (all very dependent on the orientation of your snow hole relative to wind direction. Our hole was facing away from the anticipated incoming storm. Maybe better to have it at an angle, definitely not facing into the wind!) However, you’re always limited by terrain features dictating where you dig). Still quite a lot of snow was coming in and I realised I would need to set my alarm for every hour to shovel out. I had two clients with me and we had agreed the before bed to take turns clearing checking. Given the gravity of the situation I decided as the guide that I should be checking all night and that’s what I did. The blizzard abated somewhat in the early hours but still blowing probably 30-50mph in the morning (similar weather conditions to White Mountains in winter). We navved out, around 5 miles in a whiteout, sideways wind occasionally blowing us over, on bearings with a hand held compass (no GPS watch or smart phone or power bank, not that I could afford anyway, back in 2010. Tech probably wouldn’t hold up to those conditions anyway). 

A little close to misadventure and a good lesson. The snow storm was worse than they had forecast but that is also something to note. I guess forecasting has improved in 15 years but they can still get in wrong, often in anticipating how fast or slow a front will move. Play it safe. 

One other comment mentioned digging in a snow bank to allow gravity to assist in the digging and so cold air can escape and travel down the slope. This is correct in my experience.  If possible (not always if you haven’t got a convenient snow bank) I think it’s better to avoid creating a cold sink where air is trapped.

def fibDPTabulation(position):
    if position <= 1: return 1
    table = list()
    table = [0 for i in range(0, position+1)]
    table[1] = 1
    
    length = len(table)
    for i in range(2, length):
        table[i] = table[i-2] + table[i-1]
    
    return table[position]

5:25:43 The reason as to why you got the same value is because of how IPython and randomness work.
So, if anyone wondering:
Computers aren't built for randomness and they can't just generate a random number. So instead they are generating quasi-random numbers based on a seed. Basically, just applying a series of mathematical operations on a "seed" to get a number. Then, generated number becomes new seed.
Now what is happening here: as you will get the same "random" number from the same seed, that means next seed will be the same as previous generation. This means with the same seed you are getting same series of numbers!
IPython (Interactive Python) is basically just running program. And it saves the seed. It means that after generating those  2 tensors you will get the seed for generating number 0.2345 EVERY time.  BUT, if you continue to generate, number will be gone.
Simple way to test this is to reset the seed (42), regenerate those tensors and generate the number again. It will be 0.2345. If they hadn't changed randomness algorithm by the time you are reading this.

CommentText:
I think an easier way to do this is too find the position of N and delete it. One way to do this is too take the length of the llist and subtract N from it. This will give us the position. We iterate through again and once our current position is less than the target position ( len_llist - N), that we can connect the links accordingly.  I don't know how much this makes sense writing it, but here is the solution I came up with: 

class Solution:
    def removeNthFromEnd(self, head: Optional[ListNode], n: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:


        ll_len = 0
        curr = head
        while curr:
            ll_len += 1
            curr = curr.next
        
        prev = None
        curr_pos = 0
        target = ll_len - n
        # reset curr 
        curr = head

        if ll_len == n:
            head = curr.next

        while curr and curr_pos < target:
            prev = curr
            curr = curr.next
            curr_pos += 1
        
        if prev:
            prev.next = curr.next

        
        return head

CommentText: Flexbox is a relatively new technique that simplifies the design of responsive layouts. It includes various properties for the Flexbox container and specific properties for the items within it. It is very straightforward :- Flexbox properties include: 1/ flex-direction: column or column-reverse, which arranges items in a column or in reverse order; alternatively, flex-direction: row or row-reverse arranges items in a row or in reverse order. 2/ flex-wrap: wrap or nowrap, which determines whether items wrap to the next line or not. 3/ flex-flow is a shorthand property for the previous two values. The remaining properties, 4, 5, and 6, relate to positioning and order. 4/ justify-content: takes values such as a. center; which centers items, b. flex-start; which aligns items to the start, c. flex-end; which aligns items to the end, d. space-between; which evenly distributes space between items, with no space at the edges, e. space-around; which evenly distributes space around items. 5/ align-items: This property aligns and positions items vertically within the flexbox container, with several values: a. center (centers items), b. flex-start (aligns to the start), c. flex-end (aligns to the end), d. stretch (stretches items to fill the container), e. baseline (aligns items along their baselines, regardless of size). 6/ align-content: This property is similar to justify-content but manages the spacing between new lines created when items wrap due to a small screen size. It specifically affects the spacing between lines, and it accepts the same values as justify-content. Secondly, properties for items within the flexbox: These properties are written within the style of the element itself. Each item within the flexbox is treated as a primary "Base Child," and all primary children are automatically flexed. The flex item properties: 1. order: This property allows you to rearrange the position of elements without physically moving them. You simply assign a new order number, such as moving the fourth element to the first position. 2. flex-grow: You specify a value for the number of times you want the element to grow relative to other elements. 3. flex-shrink: When there are too many elements, they shrink within the container. You can set the value to "0" to prevent a specific element from shrinking, ensuring it remains its original size. 4. flex-basis: 200px; specifies that the initial value must be 200 pixels and should not be less, but it can be more. This property sets a condition that the selected element's size should not be less than the given value. 5. flex is shorthand for the preceding property values, allowing you to write values in the order mentioned. Only values. 6. align-self: center, flex-start, or flex-end are the three values it accepts. Its function is specific to an element within the flexbox, controlling its position and placement within the container—whether it is at the top, in the middle, or at the bottom. Thank you very much.

CommentText: I started programming with Logo and Basic (not VB) in the mono-monitor days on a Vic-20 and Apple IIe. Then moved to Pascal and C (on PC clones). I used to love creating multimedia projects using Director back in the day (early 90s). Combined with Photoshop and Illustrator, the trio revolutionized presentations and interactivity. CommentText: I'd like to point out that modern C++ versions recommend the use of Smart Pointers, which alleviates many memory management concerns. This is similar to how Rust handles it, but in an optional manner, as far as I understand. Also, I fail to see how anyone could consider Rust easier. It's incredibly obscure and tries too hard to be concise, which makes it harder to grasp. I tried Rust, and I disliked it. Generally, I am not a fan of how recently every Tom, Dick, and Harry decided they were gurus and should create their own programming language, leading to a multitude of redundant and unnecessary languages (Go, Rust, Ruby, etc.). Consequently, the development field is very disorganized. You join a company, and every tool they utilize is written in a distinct language – C, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Go, Python, QT… Then they employ scripts to try and bring all of this chaos together. Don't misunderstand me, there is a place for new languages when they truly bring unique advantages. But many are simply 'We're doing the same thing, but our way!'. It's messy, and I hate it.

Angular and React are both great. I'm ok with your personal preference, but not with the misleading information. It is not black and white.

CommentText: Entity: Anything we store data about. Attribute: The specifics we store. E.g.: Entity-Person, Attribute-Name, Age, Gender. Entity Type: The particular person referred to. Attribute Type: The specific column being referenced. Database Design: 1. Conceptual 2. Logical 3. Physical. Progressing from 1 to 3, we transition from a general to a specific design. Data Integrity: 1. Entity Integrity: How to uniquely identify each user/record. 2. Referential Integrity: Integrity in tables with relationships. 3. Domain Integrity: Refers to the integrity of column values. E.g., a PhoneNo column cannot contain alphabets. Designing 1:1 relationships: This can be achieved in 2 ways: 1. Attribute: All data is stored in a single table. For instance, if we have user data and their credit card number, we keep it in one table with only one extra column, and the table remains about the user. 2. Entity: Two tables are maintained. Using the previous example, if we also want to store the date of issue, expiry date, CVV, etc., putting it in one table would make it about both users and cards, so we create two separate tables: one with user info and the card number (or a unique ID for the card), and another with card information. Keys: 3 main points: 1) Unique 2) Never Changing 3) Never NULL. Superkey: Any number of columns needed to ensure each row is unique. Candidate key: The fewest number of columns needed to ensure each row is unique. Multiple columns can potentially make a row unique, such as username or email address. Choose the column that meets the 3 criteria of KEYS; that is your primary key. The others become your candidate key. Natural Key: A primary key column available in the table with real-world value, like a username. Surrogate Key: A primary key column not available in the table and without real-world value. We add this column to the table, like an auto-incremental ID. Foreign Key Constraint: Action: 1) On Update 2) On Delete. Type: 1) Restrict (No Action): An error is thrown. 2) Cascade: The action is reflected in FK columns. 3) Set NULL: Values in the FK column are set to NULL. Compound Key: A key made up of multiple columns, where all columns are keys themselves. Modality: Indicates whether the FK is nullable or not, denoted by nullable(1) and not nullable(0), essentially stating that at least 0 or 1 values are required. ( ) for quick revision. Database Normalization: 1NF: 1) Columns should have atomic (single) values. 2) There should be no duplicates. 2NF: 1) Must be in 1NF. 2) There should be no partial dependency. Point 2: If a primary key isn't composite, it's automatically in 2NF. If composite, and a non-key column in a table depends on partial columns of the composite key (i.e., not dependent on all columns forming the composite key), it's not in 2NF, and we need to create a separate table to remove this. 3NF: 1) Must be in 2NF. 2) There should be no transitive dependency. Indexes: If you have an index on two columns (ln and fn), then in the WHERE clause: 1) Using both ln and fn will hit the index. 2) Using only ln (being on the left) will hit the index. 3) Using only fn (being on the right) will not hit the index. Points 2 & 3 work in MySQL; verification is needed for other Databases.

I'm 36 and I mostly have ADD. 
I really struggled to pay attention to the teachers in school. When they were giving instructions to the class, my mind would wander, and when I finally snapped back; everyone would be working and I wouldn't have a clue what to do. It usually ended with me not having produced any work and the teacher pulling me to the front of the class to scream at me. To say this situation was stressful was an understatement. Everytime the teacher started giving instructions, I would be internally screaming at myself to stay focused. Listen to what they're saying. I would be panicking like crazy. But, it just seemed completely out of my control and my mind would inevitably wander. I hated it. Because I was shouted at every single time, my classmates started bullying me as well. I always felt like something was wrong with me. Led me to have a very deep depression and self hatred. Having a diagnosis finally allowed me to overcome depression, after suffering for years.

Would just like to add, that as an adult my ADD symptoms are practically non-existent. Definitely not completely gone, but I'm more than capable of staying focused to instructions now. But, the treatment I received as a kid, carried with me into adulthood, and I hated myself regardless of the improvement. It's crazy how such mistreatment as a child, can severely affect your adult life.

That means one of these whiz bang quantum gizmos drift about 3 feet in an hour.  That's about the accuracy of GPS.  That means after an hour, these devices get progressively worse than GPS. So when you fly your B2 bomber halfway around the world over 15 hours and drop your precision guided bomb on a target, your targeting accuracy will be about 15 times worse than GPS.    By the time your B2 makes it back to base and attempts to land in zero visibility, it'll be off enough to completely miss the runway. CommentText:
What's important to understand about assembly language is that it's a direct 1:1 with machine code. When you program in assembly you are also explicitly programming in machine code, since every opcode has a defined mnemonic. The programmer choses the required mnemonic (and operand if required) for each statement. The assembler simply looks up each opcode from each mnemonic, adding appropriate operands when present. It's a virtually instant process.
Compilation is entirely different. What is very frequently overlooked when dealing with compiled languages is that feeding the same source code (in the same IDE on on the same PC) through different compilers will almost always produce different machine code. This can have a very significant bearing on executable size and execution speed. One compiler may also introduce bugs in the machine code that are not picked up till much later.
It's highly recommended, particularly for C/C++ programmers, to have an expert level ability in assembly language. Only then will you be fully able to critically analyse/troubleshoot/debug any assembly produced from the compilation process. A C/C++ programmer with little/no assembly skills is handicapped to extremes - yes, they can code in C/C++ but absolutely no, their debugging will be spectacularly lacking.

Just remember that Trump’s rhetoric is backed by the intelligence community, even if it is riddled with questionable facts. In the context of an undeclared World War III, he is positioning the United States much as it did during WWI and WWII.

If the U.S. were to reclaim control of the Panama Canal, it would provoke international outrage. Panama has safeguarded the canal through neutrality—much like Switzerland—earning global trust. Any U.S. move to take over would destabilize the region and likely backfire, creating diplomatic and logistical challenges. I'd like to remind everyone that the Torrijos-Carter Treaty was more than just the turnover of the canal, but an effort backed up by most Latin American militaries to get Southern Command and the US military bases out of Panama.

As a Panamanian, I observed how President Juan Carlos Varela (2014–2019) broke diplomatic relations with Taiwan and established them with China. This move led to considerable Chinese investment in the country, which prompted a visit by then–U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo to the presidential palace. Ultimately, many Chinese-backed projects were either canceled or only partially completed, including a Chinese Embassy at the entrance of the Canal.

The Chinese do not own or operate the Panama Canal. However, they do hold a recently renewed concession for ports on both the Caribbean and Pacific sides of Panama—something the United States views as a strategic threat to the canal. In modern warfare, drones and other high-tech weaponry can be hidden inside seemingly innocuous shipping containers, ready to launch attacks on critical infrastructure at a moment’s notice.

I understand my fellow Panamanians who emphasize that the Panama Canal is on sovereign Panamanian territory. Yet the Torrijos-Carter Treaty has clauses that allow the U.S. to retake control of the canal operations if global supply chains or U.S. naval movements are threatened—whether through water mismanagement, sabotage, or civil unrest affecting the canal’s functioning.

If such a takeover were to happen, it would likely not resemble the 1989 invasion, which was aimed at dismantling the Panamanian Defense Force and capturing Manuel Noriega. Instead, it might look more like an American-appointed board of directors working closely with Panamanian counterparts to keep the canal operational—removing private or oligarchic interference within the Panama Canal Authority.

As taken from the book Guarding the Crossroads: “United States military interest in the Panama Canal is in its use, not its ownership. Therefore, any new treaty must assure that access to and security of the Panama Canal are protected in times of war and peace. CommentText: I don't mean to be negative, and I generally agree with Jeff Rosen. However, as a German professional in the German correctional system, I'd like to clarify a few points, mainly arising from the specific type of prison Mr. Rosen visited. Heidering prison is a modern, cutting-edge facility. Other prisons in Germany are far less appealing, with older buildings, limited natural light from high windows, and no cafeterias like the one shown. In some German prisons, many inmates spend extended periods (up to 23 hours) in their cells, often without individual cells. Additionally, inmates typically receive the same meals and don't prepare their own food daily; cooking is a recreational activity done occasionally. The availability of sports, recreation, and opportunities to leave the prison for external activities (like doctor visits, therapy, or seeing loved ones) varies significantly, ranging from extensive options like at Heidering to almost none (except for medical emergencies, under armed guard) in older prisons. It heavily depends on the prison directorate's approach, whether they are modern and rehabilitation-focused or more traditional, emphasizing punishment and correction. Therefore, Mr. Rosen presented the best, most advanced, and rehabilitation-oriented standard of the German system. Heidering is not representative of a typical German prison. Nevertheless, his core arguments remain valid. Even the most outdated, punishment-focused prisons in Germany (which are decreasing as older directors retire and are replaced by more open-minded individuals) are generally more pleasant than typical US facilities, as even the minimum legal standards in German prisons grant inmates certain rights likely uncommon in US correctional facilities. Apologies for any grammatical or spelling errors; English isn't my native language.

In TypeScript, if an array is declared as readonly, you cannot use the push method to add new elements to it. This is because the readonly modifier prevents any modifications to the array.
Instead, you can use the spread operator (...) to create a new array with the additional elements, like this:
TypeScript
let arr: readonly number[] = [1, 2, 3];
arr = [...arr, 4, 5]; // creates a new array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

CommentText: One of the best movies ever, i got to enjoy going to the salt flats in Bonneville many years ago when i was just 19 and it was amazing both for the racing and beauty. The team i was with was going for record in one of the 4 cylinder classes but its been a few years so don't remember all the details:), Just like in the movie and most motorsports the people there were super nice plus awesome sportsmanship. Since i was dealing with engine and engine electronics i was pretty busy the whole time but a night its one of the most beautiful places i have ever been too, the sky is breathtaking and u can see so much since there is hardly any light pollution. We ended up getting the time we were after and actually slightly better than planned, second to last run i made a huge change to ECM and that's what it needed to get us there even though when we tore engine down later it was starting to nuke a exhaust valve but held on long enough. I knew EGT's were gonna get up there to the limit but sometimes u just have to send it and take the chance for the glory:), once we accomplished our goal things were way more chill and had the time to hang out with other teams too. Learned so much while there and got to see some amazing cars/bikes too, always wanted to go back but after a year with the team i was with the  plans changed and i ended up going to their race shop doing pretty much the same thing i was but no more speed records. Being a mechanic all my life plus a cool computer geek allowed me to really learn car electronic systems from the early days of multiport injection, it paid off cause cars are rolling computer networks now and most mechanics run when it comes to wiring/modules/electronics. The team took me on so young because of my knowledge of tuning/vehicle computer systems, it was actually my machine shop guy that recommended me too them who was another great dude that taught me so much. Will always be thankful for that trip and it was a once in a lifetime type deal cause i could never afford the trip or have a car worthy of the flats, totally understand the addiction of speed and the speed records but its a rich mans game now just like many other forms of motorsport. Sucks but money makes everything happen and whoever has the most money wins, even with restrictions to limit this we all know more money is needed to engineer around the rules some for a advantage. CommentText: This video is incredibly useful and informative; however, there's a minor inaccuracy that might cause some confusion. You mentioned utilizing a 'third method' for installing create-nuxt-app via NodeJS, but you were actually using NPM, which is indeed a part of NodeJS, along with NPX. By using NPM to run create-nuxt-app, you're essentially running the locally stored version of create-nuxt-app from when it was installed globally. NPX functions similarly to NPM -g, but it always fetches the latest version and runs it once. If you have a fast internet connection, NPX is generally preferable. If your internet isn't as fast, NPM might be a better option, but you'll be using an older version.

CommentText: It's quite common to encounter data that's already sorted or nearly sorted. Therefore, using the last element as the pivot in this implementation is not optimal. While many suggest picking a random element and swapping it with the last, this still results in quadratic time complexity for arrays with identical elements. A better approach is to track the last index less than the pivot and use that for the left window, instead of p-1. This avoids redundant processing of pivot duplicates. For instance: class Solution: def findKthLargest(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int: n = len(nums) k = n - k def quickselect(l, r): pivotIndex = random.randint(l, r) nums[pivotIndex], nums[r] = nums[r], nums[pivotIndex] pivot = nums[r] p = l lessEnd = -1 for i in range(l, r): num = nums[i] if num < pivot: lessEnd = p if num <= pivot: nums[p], nums[i] = nums[i], nums[p] p += 1 nums[p], nums[r] = nums[r], nums[p] if k > p: return quickselect(p+1, r) elif k > lessEnd: return nums[p] else: return quickselect(l, lessEnd) return quickselect(0, n-1)

CommentText:
Although there are some good explanations already on why we move the pointer with the lower height inward, here is another perspective. 

The objective of the problem is to maximize min(heights[a], heights[b]) *⋅* (b - a). We start off the problem with the pointers at the edges. If either pointer moves inward, that second term (b - a) is always going to decrease, so that is out of our control. 

But if we move the higher-height pointer inward, the first term min(heights[a], heights[b]) can only decrease or remain fixed. To see why, note that there are two cases: 1) The higher-height pointer reaches an even higher height—since we are taking the min, the term will remain the same; 2) We reach a lower height—then the term may either stay fixed or decrease if it is lower than the other pointer's height.

On the other hand, moving the lower-height pointer inward, there are once again two cases: 1) The lower-height pointer reaches a higher height, then the term will always increase; 2) We reach a lower height, then the term decreases.

So in order to maximize the first term, min(heights[a], heights[b]), we must move the lower-height pointer inward, as moving the higher-height pointer inward yields only decreases (or fixed).
(note that the second term (b - a) is ensured to be as max as it can as we start the pointers at the edges, and move inward (thereby decreasing the term) to check for potential maximums, while keeping a max variable).

Simplified version with one var matches and 
  # Here idea is same as before problem
        # Start with window, form a first substring with matches 
        # if matches == t_maches, then try to shrink the string to min by left += 1
        # else go with right += 1

def minWindow(self, s: str, t: str) -> str:
        t_map = dict(Counter(t))
        t_map_len = len(t_map)
        left_ind = right_ind = matches = 0
        res = float("inf")
        res_str = ""

        n = len(s)
        s_map = defaultdict(int)

        while right_ind < n:
            ch = s[right_ind]
            s_map[ch] += 1

            if (ch in t_map) and s_map[ch] == t_map[ch]:
                matches += 1
            
            if matches == t_map_len:
                while left_ind <= right_ind and left_ind < n and matches == t_map_len:
                    if (right_ind - left_ind) + 1 < res:
                        res = (right_ind - left_ind) + 1
                        res_str = s[left_ind : right_ind + 1]

                    ch = s[left_ind]

                    if (ch in t_map) and s_map[ch] == t_map[ch]:
                        matches -= 1

                    s_map[ch] -= 1
                    left_ind += 1
            
            right_ind += 1

        return res_str

CommentText:
One night my VERY drunk husband passed out on the couch & left a pot boiling on the stove. I was 9 months pregnant & woke up to a house filled with smoke so thick I had to crawl on the floor to breath or see. 
After the water boiled away in the pot, a fire had started on the stove that got so hot it melted the pot & cracked the glass stovetop. 
When I dragged my barely conscious husband out of the house to safety, he tried to go back in FOUR TIMES!
After the 4th attempt, I slapped him hoping it would wake him up enough to realize what was happening & quit fighting me. I had opened both front & back doors to air it out, but it was still so thick u couldn't see more than a foot inside, let alone get enough air to breathe properly.  
After I slapped him, all he did was look at me & say, " U slapped me."
I tried to explain AGAIN the house wasn't safe til it aired out. My husband only seemed to care about the fact I slapped him & I wouldn't let him go back inside.  After that, went inside,  laid back down on the couch &  passed out again; coughing the whole time. 
I gave up on him then. I had done my best & failed. He would only have himself to blame if his lungs hurt the next day, or worse yet; were damaged. I waited outside fuming,  until the house was mainly aired out.  I then went back to bed & did my best to go back to sleep. 
The next day I didn't even get a sheepish apology for almost burning our house down! All I got was, "You hit me last night".
That's the ONLY time I've hit my partner, but I still feel guilt over it. 
Was I in the wrong even if it was the last thing I could think of to wake him? Even under a possible life & death situation, the rule still holds that it's wrong to have slapped him? Should I have just let him go back inside instead?
Or was I justified cuz I was making a last ditch attempt to wake him up enough to realize the danger?
I had already pulled, cajoled, yelled, begged & even threatened to slap him, before actually slapping him. I literally couldn't think of anything else to try. 
Before judging too harshly please take into account that I had just been pulled out of deep sleep myself &  immediately had to deal with part of my house being on fire. I was in a terrified & desperate state of mind.

4 Key points: 

1) Approach
-Think of speaking as a positive opportunity to share your ideas with people
2) Audience
-What does your audience need to know from you? What do they already know? What do they expect of you? What's their attitude about your topic?
3)Context
-Context is important: What time is it? What emotional state is your audience in? What emotional state do you want to put them in? Where are you physically?
4) Structure
Structure your talk to keep people engaged! Try:
a) Past - Present - Future: This is what the situation was, here is what it is now, here's how we want to change the situation for the future
b)Problem - solution - benefit: Here's the problem we're facing. Here's the solution I recommend. Here's the benefit to be expected
c)What - so what? - now what? : Here's the issue. Here's why you should care. Here's what we should do.

CommentText: 08:40 Jeff, no offense, but this is a baseless tangent. We have retail Steam games with data discs around here, or at least had them until very recently, apparently far longer than USA wanted them. The decompression of those was pretty much as CPU intensive as Steam downloads at the time, for similar reasons - the DVD drives aren't fast, more uncompressed data means more DVDs (and more swaps), and the CPU is presumably not doing anything else when gamer wants a new game, so might as well use it (especially back when they couldn't throttle). And this wasn't specific to Steam games, the installers of older PC games tried their best to do the same thing. So do PlayStation ones since they started installing as a standard, in spite of those dedicated decompression circuits in PS5. Discs have advantages sometimes, but they do nothing to prevent intense emulated installation decompression computing.

CommentText: It is actually more straightforward than it appears. You can instruct (not everything, but certain aspects of these) your children. During childhood, we committed a small multiplication table to memory (with only a few exceptions that can be derived more readily than recalling the answer). Consequently, we memorize the results of over 50 distinct multiplication combinations (though some might argue about simple cases like multiplications by one, suggesting these don't require memorization). The key is that it's so ingrained in us that we don't even recognize it as something we actively learned. And you can replicate this with the square of a two-digit number. It involves roughly the same quantity of combinations as a small multiplication table. And indeed, some of them need not be memorized but can instead be derived (like 10^2). This individual simply learns a bit more and extends it to a 3-digit number. And with a "table" of fewer than 100 combinations (which is not substantial if you consider it), he squares numbers with 6 digits just as swiftly as a regular child can multiply two numbers with 3 digits (half the quantity) using knowledge of a small multiplication table.

def binary_search(nums, num):
    begin_index = 0
    end_index = len(nums) - 1

    while begin_index <= end_index:
        #import pdb;pdb.set_trace
        mid_point = (begin_index + (end_index - begin_index)//2)
        mid_point_value = nums[mid_point]
        if mid_point_value == num:
            return mid_point
        elif num < mid_point_value:
            end_index = mid_point - 1
        else:
            num > mid_point_value
            begin_index = mid_point + 1
    return None

CommentText: For Windows users, it's actually simpler than it looks. Just input the database name when prompted. In the shell, it appears as follows: - Server [localhost]: Database [postgres]: test Port [5433]: Username [postgres]: Password for user postgres:your_pw - Keep in mind that the first time you connect, you're connecting to the default database, which is why you don't need to enter a name. It's named "postgres", and the owner is also default, likely "postgres". - When you log in with empty parameters, you'll see a line in the terminal like "postgres=#". The part before "=#" indicates the database name, so in this default case, it's "postgres". - He mentions the owner being "amigoscode" (when listing all databases), which is an added role. Check the Postgres documentation on how to add roles and change table owners. - Also, when you are in the "postgres=#" database, you can easily switch to another database (that already exists; it won't create one). Use the command: \c another_database_name (e.g., "postgres=# \c test" results in "test=#").

I was a fact checker for facebook. I have some information you might be interested in. Upvote this, and maybe itll be seen by whoever is reading the messages for Crowder.

 I work for a company named Appen, and we are contracted by Facebook to fact check. The way they choose who among us are chosen: There is a sort of PDF pamphlet in which they have you read for about 20 minutes to learn the fact checking system, but also to understand what they expect of us.  Following this, is a test, which takes about an hour but you could do it in 30 minutes.  The test is multiple choice, and often just true or false.  The questions are all opinion based, and even tells you there is no right or wrong answer.  However, all the questions are political in some way shape or form, and if you don't answer the way a leftist would answer, you "fail" the test. I proved this, as I failed the initial test, by answering truthfully an honestly.  The questions are things like "Is race a political issue" and of course, the answer must be yes.  You cannot express any other opinion, you absolutely must answer yes.  The second time I took the test, I entered it under another name, created a new profile to submit for authentication, and was accepted, and took the test, answering as a leftist would answer, and I passed. 

So, thats my background.  Now I want to tell you what I know.  We were given directive from administration on how to "fact check"  Here are some of the things we were told:
1) Any conservative or 'right leaning' posts must be flagged. Cite any webpage you can find, reputable or not, and link it to the flag. It doesn't matter if its true, it doesnt matter if you believe it.
2) Any democratic or left leaning posts, you do not flag. For any reason.  The question was asked, what if it breaks the law such as death threats? The answer was, "For any reason."

I also want to talk a little bit about Zuckerburg.  He plead to the court that he was not in charge of the fact checkers.  That they are contracted "By Facebook" <-- not him directly, and that he has no control over it.  This is how he is trying to get around the law, by saying he isnt responsible, even though he has direct control over facebook.  I also want to point out, that when he gave a list of his 3rd party contractors, he did not list Appen or our competitor company Lionbridge whom is also involved though I cannot confirm to what degree, I would guess at the very least they are just as involved as we are, numbering in the thousands. Yes, there's thousands of people hired to be fact checkers. Just from my company.
